first_design.rule:
Ending a value runs its `drop` at one point of one thread. At that point it counts as a call of the `drop` for every rule: locks held, walks, views and contracts.

(1) Where the program's text fixes the point (the end of a block or a statement, a replacement, a `clear()`, the line that ends the last owner), the call is checked there. A clash is refused with the line to write.

(2) Where the compiler or the runtime picks the point (a `thread_shared` value queued back to the thread that made it, or the fields a reload removes), it picks only a clear point. A clear point is one where that call, written there, would be accepted by every rule, and where the thread holds no lock at all if the drop may take one. So a placed drop never waits for its own thread's lock, never changes a walked list, never breaks a contract, and never adds an order between locks that the program did not write. It runs at the first clear point the thread reaches.

(3) Some threads are at rest: a thread that has ended, has returned from its outermost Ember call to C, waits for work in the job system, or sleeps in a blocking call made at a clear point. Such a thread first empties its queue. While it rests, the thread that ends the last owner of one of its values ends that value at once, at a line `[THR-20]` already checks as running the drop.

Nothing is refused for an end the compiler places. The programmer writes nothing.
first_design.spec_text:
Adds `[RC-8]`, `[RC-4]` point 6 and `[JOB-6]`. Changes `[RC-4]` points 1, 2, 3 and 5, `[OBJ-1]` (the home field), `[WK-3]`, `[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-1]`, `[THR-20]`, `[THR-16]`, `[FFI-22]`, `[HR-2a]`, `[RT-8]` and the two-count row of `[COST-3]`.

* `[RC-8]` *(new)* **Where an end runs.** Ending a value runs its `drop`, and the drops of what it owns (`[DRP-8]`), at one point of one thread. At that point it counts as a call of those drops for every rule that checks a call: a lock this thread holds (`[THR-19]`), a walk (`[BRW-18]`), a view (`[BRW-17]`, `[RC-5]`), the contracts of the functions running (§X.2), and any other rule that checks a call.
  1. **A point the source fixes.** These ends are checked as calls where the source puts them: the end of a block for its locals (`[DRP-2]`), the end of a statement for its temporaries (`[DRP-3]`), a value replaced, a collection cleared, `mem.drop`, and the line that ends a value's last owner. A clash is refused there with the line to write (`E7018`, `E3020`, `E3060`, or the contract's code). Example: a `Conn` whose `drop` takes `pool.lock` is made inside `with pool.lock:`. It ends at the end of the block, so that point is `E7018`. The message says to make the `Conn` above the `with` line, or to end it with `mem.drop(owns c)` below the block.
  2. **A point the compiler or the runtime picks.** This covers a `thread_shared` value queued to its making thread (`[RC-4]`) and the removed fields a reload reclaims (`[HR-2a]`). Such a value is ended only at a **clear point**, which has two conditions:
     * a call of its drops, written there, would be accepted by every rule of the first paragraph, with the queue's work counted as `Nondet` (which values it ends depends on other threads);
     * if one of those drops may take a lock, this thread holds none: no `with` block of a `Lock`, no `Mutex` or `RwLock` guard, no `Once` initialiser, none of the runtime's own locks.

     The drops that decide this are those of every type whose values may be queued to the thread; the compiler may use every such type in the program. So no line is ever refused for such an end. It never waits for a lock its own thread holds, it adds no order between locks that the program does not write, and it is part of no function's effects or summary (`[EFF-1]`).
  3. **When.** Such an end runs at the first clear point its thread reaches after it becomes due (`[RC-4]` point 3), or at once while that thread is at rest (`[RC-4]` point 6). A thread may stay where no point is clear: it holds a lock for ever, or runs for ever under a contract its queued drops would break. It then keeps its queued values until it leaves. No thread could run a drop that takes the held lock any sooner without waiting for that lock.

* `[RC-4]` *(changed)*
  1. ... "Only the making thread reads both, or a thread that has taken its queue while it is at rest (point 6)."
  2. ... "marking it queued in the same atomic step as its subtract. Only the queue's processing then ends it: the making thread's, or, while that thread is at rest, the processing of the thread that took its queue (point 6)."
  3. **Check points.** The compiler places them, only at clear points (`[RC-8]`):
     * at every loop's back edge;
     * before every call that may block the thread;
     * where a lock's `with` block, a walk, or a call of a function under a contract the queued drops would break ends, if it kept a point out;
     * before each job a job worker runs;
     * when the thread ends, returns from its outermost Ember call to C, or waits for work.

     A function called while this thread holds a lock, or called from a function under such a contract, runs no check point during that call. A direct call goes to a copy of the function that has none, as verdict 88 makes a copy. A call through a function value or a `dyn` or `virtual` method, or a foreign call that may run the callbacks C keeps (`[FFI-52]`), sets a mark on the thread for the length of the call, and the points test it. At each point the thread tests its queue. When the queue holds values, the thread empties it there (point 2), and their `drop`s run there.
  5. **So a value's end is delayed only** when three things hold: its last owner ends on a thread that did not make it; the value was not handed over at a place of point 4 (it travelled inside another object); and its making thread is not at rest. It is then ended at its making thread's next check point, the first clear point that thread reaches. Until then it is intact, and a `weakref` link opened on another thread may still find it (`[WK-3]`).
  6. *(new)* **A thread at rest.** A thread is at rest when it has ended, has returned from its outermost Ember call to C, waits for work in the job system, or waits inside a blocking call made at a clear point. It first empties its queue. It stays at rest until it runs Ember code again, and meanwhile it reads and writes no home count.
     * Another thread that puts a value in its queue takes that queue (one compare-and-exchange), adds the value's home count into its away count, ends the value when the sum is zero, and gives the queue back. The value's `drop` then runs at that thread's line that ended the last owner, which `[THR-20]` already checks as possibly running it.
     * A thread leaving rest takes its queue back (one compare-and-exchange), and waits while another thread holds it.

     This replaces point 3's sentence "A value whose making thread has ended is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner": an ended thread is at rest for good.

* `[OBJ-1]` *(changed)* The `home` field: "read and written only by that thread, with plain instructions; read by a thread that has taken that thread's queue while it is at rest (`[RC-4]` point 6)".

* `[WK-3]` *(changed)* The last sentence becomes: "... that was not handed over, is ended at its making thread's next check point, the first clear point it reaches (`[RC-4]` points 3 and 5), and its `drop` runs there; while that thread is at rest, the thread that ends its last owner ends it at once (`[RC-4]` point 6)."

* `[DRP-8]` *(changed)* Adds: "The end counts as a call of the `drop` at the point where it runs, the locks it may take included (`[THR-19]`). Where the compiler or the runtime picks that point, `[RC-8]` says which."

* `[EFF-1]` *(changed)* Adds: "An end that `[RC-8]` point 2 runs at a point the compiler or the runtime picks is part of no function's effects or summary. It runs only where every rule accepts it, so no contract and no caller ever sees it."

* `[THR-20]` *(changed)* "A `drop` runs where the last owner ends, or, for a value queued to its making thread, at a clear point of that thread (`[RC-8]`)." The rest is unchanged.

* `[THR-16]` *(changed)* "When `main` returns, its locals end and it empties its queue (`[RC-4]`). Then the process ends: other threads stop without running destructors, no static is freed and no other drop runs. `process.exit` ends the process at once: no drop runs and no queue is emptied."

* `[JOB-6]` *(new)* "A job worker tests its queue before each job and empties it before it waits for work. While it waits it is at rest (`[RC-4]` point 6), so a value it made is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner."

* `[FFI-22]` *(changed)* Adds: "When a thread's outermost Ember call returns to C, the thread empties its queue and is at rest (`[RC-4]` point 6) until it calls into Ember again. An outermost call whose code may make, end or open an owner of a `thread_shared` value takes the queue back on entry. A call whose code may not leaves the thread at rest. `ember_rt_shutdown()` ends what is queued to each thread at rest."

* `[HR-2a]` *(changed)* "Reclaim ... and ends removed fields, running their `drop`, at a clear point (`[RC-8]`): at once at a host's poll, where no thread runs Ember code; at `std.hot.checkpoint()` when the checkpoint is a clear point for those drops, judged by `[HR-44]`'s facts of the frames below it; otherwise at the next poll."

* `[RT-8]` *(changed)* Adds: "Entering rest is a release: one exchange of the thread's queue word. Taking a resting thread's queue, and leaving rest, are acquires: one compare-and-exchange each."

* `[COST-3]` *(changed)*, the two-count row: "... a test of the thread's queue at each check point. There is no test inside a lock's `with` block, or inside a function under a contract the queued drops would break (`[RC-8]`). One exchange to enter rest and one compare-and-exchange to leave it are paid only when a job worker sleeps for lack of work, on a blocking call's sleeping path, and around an outermost call from C whose code may touch a `thread_shared` count. One thread-local add and one subtract are paid around a call through a function value, a `dyn` or `virtual` method, or a foreign call, when that call is made inside a lock or such a contract into code that has check points. Nothing is paid per object."

answers.answer:
Main's walk under `with pool.lock:` has no check point: main holds a lock and `~Conn()` takes one, so a back edge there is not a clear point. The compiler puts one where the `with` block ends, and the outer loop's back edge is one too. `Conn`'s drop runs there, on main, right after main lets the lock go. Nothing is refused and nothing is written.

If main is already waiting in `h.join()` when the worker ends `b`, main is at rest (the join is a blocking call at a clear point). The worker then ends the `Conn` at once, at the line that ends `b`. `[THR-20]` already checks that line as running `~Conn()`, and the worker holds no lock there.
answers.code:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the worker ends the Conn's last owner
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:                       # main holds a lock: no check point in here
            for id in pool.free:              # this back edge is not a clear point
                println(id)
        # the block has ended: a check point; a queued Conn's drop runs here
    println(h.join())                         # a blocking call at a clear point: main rests while it waits
answers.outcome: Compiles. While the worker runs, frames print nothing, because `pool.free` is empty. Once the worker has ended `b`, main runs `Conn`'s drop where its next `with pool.lock:` block ends: the drop takes the lock and pushes 1, and every later frame prints 1. `h.join()` prints 1. The drop never runs while main holds the lock or walks the list, so the program never hangs and the walked list never changes. If the worker finishes only while main waits in `h.join()`, the worker runs the drop itself and no frame printed 1.

answers.answer:
A job worker that waits for work is at rest (`[JOB-6]`). So is a host thread whose outermost Ember call has returned to C (`[FFI-22]`), and a thread asleep in a blocking call made at a clear point. Each first empties its queue. While it rests, the thread that ends one of its values' last owner ends that value at once.

So main's `bundles.clear()` ends each `Texture` at once if the worker that made it is already waiting. Otherwise that worker ends it before it waits. A worker also tests its queue before each job.
answers.outcome:
Compiles. "texture 1 freed" and "texture 2 freed" are printed right after `bundles.clear()`. Main prints a line during the clear if that texture's worker is already waiting; otherwise the worker that made it prints it before it waits. Then come the frames. No texture is held while the game runs.

For a host thread: a value queued to it during a callback is ended before the callback returns to C. A value queued while the thread is in C is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner.

other_cases.settled: Point 1. The block's end is a written point, checked as a call of `~Conn()`: `E7018` there. The message says to make `c` above the `with` line, so that it ends after the lock is let go, or to end it with `mem.drop(owns c)` below the block. C++'s `{ lock_guard g(m); Conn c; }` deadlocks here; Ember refuses it when compiling (verdict 43).

other_cases.settled: Point 1. The temporary ends at the statement's end (`[DRP-3]`), inside the lock: `E7018`. The fix is `c = Conn(...)` above the `with` line.

other_cases.settled: No point is placed in `mix`, or in what it calls during that call (each callee runs as a copy with none, or the thread's mark covers an indirect call), because a call of the drops there would break `@realtime`. The queue is emptied at the first clear point after `mix` returns. Nothing is refused, and `mix` keeps its contract. `@deterministic` is the same, since the queue's work counts as `Nondet`.

other_cases.settled: No point is placed inside. A placed drop that may take a lock never runs while this thread holds any lock, so the program never gets a `stats.lock`-then-`pool.lock` order it did not write (which could deadlock with a thread taking them the other way). The drop runs where the block ends. A queued drop that takes no lock (a `Texture` that only prints and frees) may run inside the block.

other_cases.case: A server's accept thread waits an hour in `listener.accept()`, at a clear point, while `Conn` values it made are ended on workers.
other_cases.settled: Point 6. On the call's sleeping path the thread empties its queue and rests. Each worker that ends a `Conn`'s last owner ends it at once, so the pool gets its connections back while the thread sleeps.

other_cases.case: A thread inside `with q.lock:` waits on `rx.recv()` while values it made are ended elsewhere.
other_cases.settled: The wait is not at a clear point because a lock is held, so the thread does not rest and the values wait in its queue. The other threads only push to the queue and go on: none of them waits for `q.lock` because of these values. The values are ended where the `with` block ends.

other_cases.case: A job worker idle for the rest of the process (pool workers end only with it, `[THR-16]`).
other_cases.settled: `[JOB-6]`: the worker rests while it waits, so every value it made is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner. A value queued while the worker runs a job is ended within that job, or before the worker next waits.

other_cases.case: A C audio driver calls an exported Ember function on its own thread. The function makes a `thread_shared Buffer`, which travels inside a `Mix` object to an Ember mixer thread, and the mixer ends it while the driver thread is back in C.
other_cases.settled: `[FFI-22]` and point 6. The driver thread emptied its queue and went to rest when the callback returned, so the mixer ends the `Buffer` at once. An exported function whose code touches no `thread_shared` count (a checksum) pays nothing on entry or on return.

other_cases.case: A callback C runs during `glfwPollEvents()`, which Ember calls inside `with ui.lock:`.
other_cases.settled: The foreign call may run the callbacks C keeps (`[FFI-52]`) and is made inside a lock, so it sets the thread's mark. No queued drop runs in the callback; the queue is emptied where the `with` block ends.

other_cases.settled: `[HR-2a]`. By `[HR-44]`'s facts a frame below holds a lock, so the checkpoint is not a clear point for that drop. The removed fields are reclaimed at the next host poll, where no thread runs Ember code. The new code still runs from the checkpoint on.

other_cases.case: Program exit: `main` returns while a worker still holds a `Conn` that main made; or `process.exit(1)` is called inside a lock.
other_cases.settled: `[THR-16]`. When main returns, its locals end, then it empties its queue (a clear point: no frame is left), then the process ends. Values queued after that, and everything other threads hold, are not ended, as for every object of another thread. `process.exit` runs no drop and empties no queue, as today. The debug leak report runs only when no other thread runs, and by then every queue is empty.

other_cases.case: A generator is abandoned mid-iteration: `g = d.replay()`, one `next`, then `g` ends.
other_cases.settled: Point 1. Its end is a written point, checked as the drops of its frame's locals (`[EFF-1]`, ODR-057). Check points inside a generator's body follow the context of the `next` call that runs them.

other_cases.case: A queued `Conn`'s drop ends the last owner of a `thread_shared Buffer` that a third thread made.
other_cases.settled: That end follows the same rule on the thread running the drop: the `Buffer` goes into its maker's queue, or is ended at once if its maker is at rest.

other_cases.case: A parent at the end of `with scope = thread.scope():`, holding no lock, while a task ends an owner of a value the parent made.
other_cases.settled: The scope's end is a blocking call at a clear point, so the parent rests while it waits. The task ends the value at once, at its own line, which `[THR-20]` checks.

other_cases.case: A static whose initialiser runs under `Once` (`[STA-3]`) contains a loop.
other_cases.settled: `Once` holds its lock while the initialiser runs, so no point is placed there for a drop that may take a lock.

other_cases.case: A `Receiver` ends while values are still queued in its channel (`[THR-15]`).
other_cases.settled: Point 1: a written end. It already ends the values after letting the channel's lock go, which is the same thing this rule requires.

other_cases.case: A later `await` (§XI.6), or any other point the compiler adds in the future.
other_cases.settled: `[RC-8]` point 2 decides it with no new text: a queued drop runs at such a point only where the point is clear.

first_design.prior_art:
**C++.** A `shared_ptr`'s destructor runs on whichever thread lets the last copy go. A destructor that locks a `std::mutex` its own thread holds is undefined behaviour. One that changes a container a range-for is walking invalidates the iterators, also undefined. Nothing checks either. C++26's hazard pointers and RCU run retired deleters at points the library picks, and the deleter's author must make it safe there.

**Rust.** `Arc`'s drop runs where the last `Arc` ends, and every thread counts atomically: that is the 25% verdict 101 measured on a thread's own objects. Locking a `Mutex` the thread already holds "might panic or deadlock" (the std docs), and this is found only when the program runs. The borrow checker keeps a drop away from a walked collection, except through `RefCell`, where it is a run-time panic. crossbeam-epoch runs deferred destructors during a later `pin()` on any thread, with no time bound: its docs say one may never run.

**Swift.** `deinit` runs at the last release, on that thread. Swift 6's isolated deinit (SE-0371) queues the deinit of an actor-isolated object released elsewhere as a job on the actor's executor, so it runs between jobs, never inside one. This is the nearest relative of the rule, but it covers actor classes only, costs an executor hop, and has no compile-time check.

**Ada.** Finalisation runs at scope exit, a point the source fixes. A potentially blocking operation inside a protected action is a bounded error (Program_Error if detected, RM 9.5.1). **Zig.** No destructors; `defer` is written.

**Go, Java, C#.** Finalisers run on a runtime thread: one goroutine in Go, the Finalizer and Cleaner threads in Java, the finalizer thread in .NET. They never clash with the code that let go, but there is a hidden thread, no bound (Go and Java say they may never run), and a collector.

**Python.** CPython runs `__del__` wherever a count reaches zero or the collector runs. Its own data-model documentation warns that a `__del__` taking a lock can deadlock on the code it interrupted.

**Objective-C/Cocoa.** An autorelease pool is drained at the top of each run-loop turn, where no application frame holds anything.

**Linux.** The last `fput()` of a file defers the release to task_work. That runs when the task returns to user mode, where it holds no kernel lock. RCU callbacks run in softirq context and must not sleep.

**JVM.** HotSpot's safepoint polls sit at loop back edges and returns (strip-mined in counted loops). They are safe because the collector runs no Java code there. Ember runs user `drop` code at its points, so a back edge is not safe for that work as such.

**Biased counting.** The paper Ember's counts come from (Choi, Shull and Torrellas, PACT 2018) leaves to the runtime when the owner thread processes its queue. The lead's report left that placement to design, and `[RC-4]` point 3 is a lead choice.

**Where each falls short.**
* C++ and Rust do not defer, so there is nothing to place. But they pay an atomic count on every thread, and they leave the self-wait and the walked container to run time, or to undefined behaviour.
* The finaliser-thread languages avoid the clash, but give no bound and need a collector.
* Swift's isolated deinit, Cocoa's pools and Linux's task_work have the right shape: run the deferred end where its home thread holds nothing. But each does it by convention, by hand, or for one kind of object.

The rule takes that shape for every end the compiler places, decides it when compiling, and keeps the two-count speed.
first_design.cost:
**Against what.** C has no deferred ends, so C pays nothing here. The relevant comparison is one atomic count (C++ `shared_ptr`, Rust `Arc`), which verdict 101's two counts beat by 25% on a thread's own objects: 32.6 ms against 43.6 ms (`measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md`). The rule keeps that gain for every type.

**Per operation.**
1. A check point outside a clash: unchanged from `[COST-3]`, one thread-local load of the queue word and a branch not taken.
2. Inside a lock's `with` block, a function under a contract the drops would break, or a walk or view they clash with: zero. There is no point there, so this is fewer tests than today.
3. Where such a region ends and it kept a point out: one thread-local load and a branch, beside the lock's own release (an atomic).
4. A direct call made inside a clash into a function that has points: zero time. The cost is one more copy of the function, in code size, as with verdict 88's copy. The copy is made only for callees that have points.
5. A call through a function value or a `dyn`/`virtual` method, or a foreign call that may run kept callbacks, made inside a clash into code that may have points: one plain thread-local add before and one subtract after. The callee's points read the mark only when the queue holds values.
6. Rest: one atomic exchange of the queue word to enter it, one compare-and-exchange to leave it. Paid only when a job worker goes to sleep for lack of work; on a blocking call's sleeping path, beside the system call that sleeps; and around an outermost call from C whose code may make, end or open an owner of a `thread_shared` value. Zero for one that may not.
7. A thread that ends a value's last owner while the value's maker rests: one compare-and-exchange to take the queue and one store to give it back, then the merge and the drop it would otherwise have queued. Only on the path that queues (a value that travelled inside another object).
8. A job worker before each job: one thread-local load and a branch.

**Memory.** Zero per object: the 32-byte header already holds the queue link. Per thread: the rest state, in spare bits of the existing queue word, and one thread-local integer for the mark.

**Where it is zero.** Every count change, every check point outside a clash, every direct call, every exported function that touches no `thread_shared` count, and every blocking call that does not actually sleep.

**Not measured:** items 6 and 7. They must be measured on the laptop (P-cores, mains) before the rule goes in, and the rest protocol stress-tested the way `stress.c` tested rule Q.

readability.note: Not a character changes: the rule adds no word, attribute or line. The same text now has one meaning. The work belongs to the compiler (where it places check points) and to the runtime (rest); the programmer never writes or sees a check point. A connection pool, a texture cache and a game loop read exactly as before. Option A would make the loop copy the list out of the lock; the rule changes nothing in the text.

first_design.compiler_does:
1. Works out, over the whole program, which `thread_shared` types may be queued. A type may be queued when a value's owner may reach another thread inside another object (by `[THR-2]`'s routes) without point 4's hand-over. For each thread's entry (main, each `thread.spawn` and job function, each export and kept callback), it also works out which of those types its code may make. It then takes the summary of the queued drops (their drop chains, `[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-24]`): the locks they may take, what they change and end, their effects, plus `Nondet`. One program-wide set is allowed.
2. Decides, from each function's own code, whether each candidate point is clear. The candidates are loop back edges, the point before a blocking call, the point before each job, thread end, the return to C, and a worker's wait. A point is clear when no lock is held (no `with` block, no guard), no walk or view is live that the drops change or end, and the function has no contract their effects would break.
3. Carries the caller's context into callees.
   * A direct call made inside a lock or a contract function goes to a copy of the callee with no points, as verdict 88's copy. The copy is made only for callees that have points.
   * A call made there through a function value, a `dyn` or `virtual` method, or a foreign call that may run kept callbacks, is bracketed by a thread-local mark, which the callee's points test on their slow path.
4. Where a lock's `with` block, a walk or a contract call kept a point out, places a point where it ends, so the bound holds.
5. Emits the rest transitions:
   * the return to C from the outermost call, only for an export or callback whose code may touch a `thread_shared` count;
   * a blocking call's sleeping path, when the call is made at a clear point;
   * the job worker's wait;
   * thread end.
6. Keeps the queue's work out of every function's effects and summary, and refuses nothing because of it.
7. Checks written ends as calls of their drops (point 1), as `[DRP-8]` and `[THR-19]` already do.
8. For hot reload, records whether each `std.hot.checkpoint()` call is a clear point, with `[HR-44]`'s facts, so that plan can defer reclaim.
9. Optionally, `ember inspect` lists each point that was left out and the lock or contract that kept it out.
first_design.misuse:
**Nothing new can be misused.** No program can write, call or skip a check point, and foreign code never reads the header (`[OBJ-1]`).

**Refused when compiling:** a written end that clashes.
* A local or a temporary ends inside `with pool.lock:`, and its drop takes `pool.lock`: `E7018`, with the line to write.
* A `clear()` inside a walk of something its drops change: `E3020`.

**Never undefined behaviour.** A drop the compiler places never runs inside a lock, a walk, a view or a contract it clashes with. So neither C++'s self-wait on a `std::mutex` (undefined) nor a walked list being changed can happen. Another thread reads a home count only while that count's thread is at rest, after a release.

**Not refused, and stated:**
* A thread that holds a lock, or runs under a contract, for ever keeps the values queued to it. No thread could run a drop that takes that lock any sooner without waiting for it.
* A queued drop that blocks (`[DRP-4]` says it should not) waits on its making thread, at a clear point. If what it waits for is held by a thread that is itself waiting for this one, both wait. A destructor that locks behaves the same in C++, Rust and Swift; lock order is checked in debug only (`[THR-4]`).
first_design.verdicts:
**43 kept.** A placed drop never runs while this thread holds a lock it may take; in fact it never runs while this thread holds any lock. A written end inside a lock, whose drop takes that lock, is refused when compiling (point 1), as 43 refuses any such call.

**56 kept.** A queued value is ended when the queue's processing finds no owner left, before its drop runs, and links then find it gone. Until then it is intact (`[RC-4]` point 5, already the text under 101). The rule shortens that window, and closes it entirely while the maker is at rest.

**57 kept, and carried to every end.** Ending a value is a call of its drop where the drop runs. For an end the compiler places, the compiler puts it only where that call is accepted, so 57 holds for queued drops with nothing refused.

**101 kept.** The two numbers stay, and the making thread deletes the value at its next check point, "placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends". The rule is the placement 101 left open: the BRC report says it is still to design, and decisions.md section 6 records the back-edge placement as a lead choice the owner may overturn.

**One widening of 101, said plainly; needs the owner's yes.** 101's "or the other thread deletes it at once if the making thread has ended" becomes "... is at rest": ended, returned to C, waiting for work, or asleep at a clear point. The evidence that it is really better:
* J7-02: a pool worker never ends, and a C thread may never call in again. Under 101's letter, a Texture's GPU memory is held for the life of the process.
* A thread at rest touches no home count, exactly like an ended one, so the same takeover is safe.
* It costs nothing on any fast path: one exchange and one compare-and-exchange, only on paths that already sleep or cross from C.

**114 kept.** An object moved to another thread has its drop run once there: a written end on that thread.

**164 to 166 untouched.** The rule relies on `[THR-8]` and `[THR-20]` (a `thread_shared` value's drop reaches only what any thread may reach), which they settle.

recommendation.reason: B is verdict 101 as written ('placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends'), with the placement 101 left open done so that no placed drop can clash. It refuses nothing: A refuses correct loops the programmer never put a point in. It loses no speed: C gives back the 25% for most types with a real drop. It needs no hidden thread, as D does, and no word from the programmer. Every queued value is ended at the first point where its making thread holds no lock and runs under no contract the drop would break, and at once while that thread is idle, in C, asleep or ended. The one change to a verdict, 'has ended' becoming 'is at rest', uses the same mechanism and closes J7-02's leak.

So `~Conn()` can run inside main's `with pool.lock:` walk, where it waits for ever for the lock main holds or changes the list main walks. owner_short.options:
A: a check point counts as a call of every queued drop, so the inner `for` under the lock is refused (E7018) and you copy the list out first.
B: the compiler puts check points only where `~Conn()` would compile and the thread holds no lock, the first one right after the clash ends; a thread that is idle, back in C, asleep or ended lets the other thread run the drop at once.
C: a type whose drop reaches outside itself, and anything a job worker or a C thread makes, is never queued; all its counts are atomic, so the worker runs `~Conn()` itself, and those types lose verdict 101's 25% on their own thread.
D: the making thread only merges the counts at a check point, and the drops run on a thread the runtime starts.
owner_short.recommendation: B: nothing refused, no word written, verdict 101's two-count speed for every type, and `~Conn()` runs on main right after main lets the lock go. It widens verdict 101's 'the making thread has ended' to 'is at rest', which needs your yes.

first_design.open_risks:
1. **A thread stuck where no point is clear never ends values queued to it.** This is a thread that holds a lock, or runs under a contract its queued drops would break, for ever.
   * For a lock, no thread could run the drop sooner without waiting for that lock.
   * For a contract (an endless `@realtime` loop on a thread that made such values earlier), another thread could, and only C or D give that.
   * The compiler could refuse the provable case: a loop no path leaves, holding the lock throughout, on a thread that may have values queued to it, as verdict 99 refuses a leak it proves. I left it out of the rule because it would catch only that trivial case.
2. **A placed drop can still meet a wait between threads.** It takes a lock on the making thread at a clear point. If another thread holds that lock while waiting for the making thread (a channel receive inside the lock), both wait. A destructor that locks behaves the same in C++, Rust and Swift. Ember checks lock order only in debug (`[THR-4]`). D avoids this at the price of a hidden thread. It belongs to a deadlock principle that no group covers.
3. **The rest protocol is a new concurrent protocol on the queue word.** It must be stress-tested the way `stress.c` tested rule Q (the race found there was in this very hand-over). The exchange and compare-and-exchange around host callbacks must be measured on the laptop (P-cores, mains) before it goes in. No number here is measured.
4. **Code size.** Copies of functions called inside locks or contracts cost code size. Where size matters, the compiler may use the mark instead, at one thread-local add and one subtract per call.
5. **Placement for speed is unchanged and unmeasured.** There is still a test at every back edge of tight loops (`[COST-3]`). Strip-mining the test, as the JVM does, would keep the bound.
6. **Coordination with other groups.**
   * P14: the queue's work is in no effect set, and is carried only where no contract forbids it.
   * P09: reclaim deferred from a checkpoint to the next poll.
   * P01: the rule relies on `[THR-8]` and `[THR-20]`, that a `thread_shared` value's drop reaches only what any thread may reach.
7. **Output from a drop may now come from main or from a worker**, depending on timing. That was already so.

method1_repair.rule:
Ending a value runs its `drop` at one point of one thread. At that point the end counts as a call of the `drop` for every rule: locks held, walks, views and contracts.

(1) Where the program's text fixes the point (the end of a block or a statement, a replacement, a `clear()`, the line that ends the last owner, on whichever thread it runs), the call is checked there. A clash is refused, with the line to write.

(2) A `thread_shared` value whose drop may wait (`Block`: a lock, a bounded `send`, a receive, a `join`, a sleep) or may call C (`FFI`) always ends at such a point. It is handed over where it is made, so the thread that ends its last owner runs the drop at that line, as C++ and Rust do. What such a drop does depends on what other threads, or C, hold when it runs, and only a line the program wrote shows that.

(3) Any other `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on another thread, after it travelled inside another object, goes back to its making thread. That thread ends it only at a clear point: one where a call of its drop, written there, would be accepted by every rule. Such a drop never waits and never calls C, so a placed end waits for nothing. Only a contract, a walk or a view can keep it out. Check points sit where a running thread reaches one after a bounded number of loop rounds, outside every such clash.

(4) A thread at rest has ended, has gone back to C, is waiting for work, or is asleep in a blocking call or in a foreign call that may block. While it rests, the thread that ends the last owner of one of its values ends that value at once, at its own line. That thread merges the counts first, and runs the drop only afterwards, with nothing of the queue held.

Nothing is refused for an end the compiler places. The programmer writes nothing.
method1_repair.spec_text:
Adds `[RC-8]`, `[RC-4]` point 6 and `[JOB-6]`. Changes `[RC-4]` points 1 to 5, `[OBJ-1]` (the home field), `[WK-3]`, `[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-1]`, `[THR-20]`, `[THR-16]`, `[FFI-22]`, `[HR-2a]`, `[HR-3b]`, `[RT-8]`, and two rows of `[COST-3]`.

* `[RC-8]` *(new)* **Where an end runs.** Ending a value runs its `drop`, and the drops of what it owns (`[DRP-8]`), at one point of one thread. At that point the end counts as a call of those drops for every rule that checks a call: a lock this thread holds (`[THR-19]`), a walk (`[BRW-18]`), a view (`[BRW-17]`, `[RC-5]`), the contracts of the functions running (§X.2), and every other rule.
  1. **A point the source fixes.** These are: the end of a block, for its locals (`[DRP-2]`); the end of a statement, for its temporaries (`[DRP-3]`); a value replaced; a collection cleared; `mem.drop`; and the line that ends a value's last owner, on whichever thread it runs (`[THR-20]`). Each end is checked as a call where the source puts it. A clash is refused there, with the line to write (`E7018`, `E3020`, `E3060`, or the contract's code). Example: a `Conn` whose `drop` takes `pool.lock` is made inside `with pool.lock:`. It ends where the block ends, before the lock is let go, so that point is `E7018`. The message says to make the `Conn` above the `with` line, so that it ends after the lock is let go.
  2. **A drop that may wait or call C runs where the source ends its value.** This covers a `thread_shared` value whose drops may wait (`Block`: a lock, a bounded channel's `send`, a receive, a `join`, a sleep, the first access to a static that another thread is initialising) or may call C (`FFI`; freeing memory is the runtime's work, `[RT-1]`, not `FFI`). Such a value is handed over where it is made (`[RC-4]` point 4): every thread counts its owners in the away count from the start. So the thread that ends its last owner ends it at that line, as C++'s `shared_ptr` and Rust's `Arc` do, and point 1 checks the end there. What such a drop does depends on what other threads, or C, hold at the moment it runs, and only a line the program wrote shows that.
  3. **A point the compiler or the runtime picks.** This covers every other `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on a thread that did not make it, and that was not handed over. Such a value is queued to its making thread (`[RC-4]`), which ends it only at a **clear point**: one where a call of its drops, written there, would be accepted by every rule of the first paragraph.
     * The drops that decide this are those of every type whose values may be queued to the thread; the compiler may use every such type in the program.
     * These drops never wait and never call C. So such an end waits for nothing and adds no order between locks. What keeps it out of a point is a contract it would break (an allocation inside `@noalloc`), or a walk or a view it would change or end.
     * No line is refused for such an end, and it is part of no function's effects or summary (`[EFF-1]`).
     * Which values a point ends depends on other threads. That alone is not `Nondet` (`[DET-6]`); whether what the drops change is `Nondet`, `[DET-2]` decides as for any code.
  4. **When.** A queued value is ended at the first clear point its making thread reaches after the value becomes due (`[RC-4]` point 3). While the making thread rests, the thread that ends the value's last owner ends it at once (`[RC-4]` point 6). A thread that runs for ever where no point is clear (an endless loop inside `@noalloc` whose queued drops allocate) keeps its queued values until it leaves that code.
  5. **A reload's reclaim.** The fields a reload removes are ended where `[HR-2a]` says, each as a call at that point.

* `[RC-4]` *(changed)*
  1. ... "Only the making thread reads both, or, while that thread rests, the one thread taking over that value (point 6)."
  2. ... "marking it queued in the same atomic step as its subtract. Only the making thread then ends it, at a clear point (`[RC-8]`), or, while the making thread rests, the thread whose subtract queued it (point 6). The making thread empties its queue at each of its check points: ..." (the rest unchanged).
  3. **Check points.** The compiler places them, only at clear points (`[RC-8]` point 3), so that a running thread never runs a loop for an unbounded number of rounds without reaching one:
     * at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts;
     * once every N rounds of a loop whose trip count is known when it starts. N is fixed by the compiler, so the rounds between two tests stay one loop that the C compiler can vectorise;
     * before every call that may block the thread, a foreign call that may block (`[EFF-3]`) included;
     * where a region that kept points out ends, if it kept one out. Such a region is a call of a function under a contract the queued drops would break, or a walk or a view they would change or end;
     * before each job a job worker runs, and when the thread ends, returns from its outermost Ember call to C, or waits for work.

     A function called from inside such a region runs no check point during that call:
     * A direct call goes to a copy of the function that has none, as verdict 88 makes a copy.
     * The following calls set a mark on the thread for the call's length: a call through a function value or a `dyn` or `virtual` method; a foreign call that may run the callbacks C keeps (`[FFI-52]`); and a call that may sleep or run jobs on this thread (a blocking call, `join`, the end of a `with scope` block, `jobs.wait`, a `@parallel` loop). Every point tests the mark, the points the runtime places included.

     At each point the thread tests its queue. When the queue holds values, the thread empties it there (point 2), and their `drop`s run there. The runtime places no point while it holds a lock of its own. A recursion with no loop reaches a point when it returns to one.
  4. ... adds: "A value whose drops may wait or call C is handed over where it is made (`[RC-8]` point 2)."
  5. **So a value's end is delayed only** when three things hold: its last owner ends on a thread that did not make it; it was not handed over, either at a place of point 4 or where it was made; and its making thread is not at rest. It is then ended at its making thread's next check point, the first clear point that thread reaches. Until then it is intact, and a `weakref` link opened on another thread may still find it (`[WK-3]`).
  6. *(new)* **A thread at rest.** A thread rests when it has ended, has returned from its outermost Ember call to C (`[FFI-22]`), waits for work in the job system (`[JOB-6]`), or sleeps inside a blocking call or a foreign call that may block. Before it rests, it empties its queue if that point is clear. A value it cannot end there stays queued until the thread's first clear point after it rests. While it rests, the thread reads and writes no home count.
     * **Code that may touch a home count** is code that may make, end or open an owner of a `thread_shared` value, end a value that owns one, or hand one over (point 4). Such code runs only after the thread has left rest.
     * **Taking over.** A thread whose subtract would queue a value to a resting thread registers as a taker of that thread's queue instead. It adds the value's home count into its away count, marks the value ended when the sum is zero, and deregisters. Only then, holding nothing of the queue, does it run the value's drops, at its own line that ended the owner; `[THR-20]` already checks that line as possibly running them. No user code runs while a taker is registered, so an end inside those drops takes the ordinary path. Several threads may take over values of one resting thread at once: rule Q gives each value to one of them, and each touches only its own value's counts and marks.
     * **Leaving rest.** A thread leaving rest first marks its queue as leaving; after that, a thread that would queue a value there pushes it as usual. The thread leaving rest then waits until no taker is registered. A taker runs a few instructions and no user code.
     * **Callbacks.** A callback that C runs while its thread rests leaves rest on entry when its code may touch a home count. When it returns, it empties its queue there (its return is a check point) and rests again. A callback whose code may not touch a home count leaves the thread at rest.

     This replaces point 3's sentence "A value whose making thread has ended is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner": an ended thread is at rest for good.

* `[OBJ-1]` *(changed)* The `home` field: "read and written only by that thread, with plain instructions; while that thread rests, by the one thread taking over that value (`[RC-4]` point 6)".

* `[WK-3]` *(changed)* The last sentence becomes: "A `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on a thread that did not make it, and that was not handed over, is ended at its making thread's next check point, the first clear point that thread reaches (`[RC-4]` points 3 and 5), and its `drop` runs there. While the making thread rests, the thread that ends the last owner ends the value at once (`[RC-4]` point 6). A value whose drops may wait or call C is handed over where it is made, and ends where its last owner ends (`[RC-8]` point 2)."

* `[DRP-8]` *(changed)* Adds: "The end counts as a call of the `drop` at the point where it runs, the locks it may take included (`[THR-19]`). For a `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on another thread, `[RC-8]` says which point that is."

* `[EFF-1]` *(changed)* Adds: "An end that `[RC-8]` point 3 runs at a point the compiler or the runtime picks is part of no function's effects or summary: it runs only where every rule accepts it."

* `[THR-20]` *(changed)* "A `drop` runs where the last owner ends, or, for a value queued to its making thread, at a clear point of that thread (`[RC-8]`). A value whose drops may wait or call C is never queued." The rest is unchanged.

* `[THR-16]` *(changed)* "When `main` returns, its locals end and it empties its queue (`[RC-4]`). Then the process ends: other threads stop without running destructors, no static is freed and no other drop runs. `process.exit` ends the process at once: no drop runs and no queue is emptied."

* `[JOB-6]` *(new)* "A job worker tests its queue before each job, and empties it before it waits for work. While it waits it is at rest (`[RC-4]` point 6), so a value it made is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner. A worker may run a job or a chunk while it waits inside another job's call (`[PAR-4]`, a scope's end). It runs that job at a point that tests the thread's mark (`[RC-4]` point 3)."

* `[FFI-22]` *(changed)* Adds: "When a thread's outermost Ember call returns to C, the thread empties its queue and rests (`[RC-4]` point 6) until it calls into Ember again. An outermost call whose code may touch a home count (`[RC-4]` point 6) leaves rest on entry; a call whose code may not leaves the thread at rest. A foreign call that may block rests the thread for its length in the same way: by its declared effects, or, when none are declared, every effect (`[EFF-3]`). A callback C runs during such a call leaves and re-enters rest as an outermost call does. `ember_rt_shutdown()` ends what is still queued to each thread."

* `[HR-2a]` *(changed)* "Reclaim frees each migrated instance's old version field by field without the type's own `drop`, since the instance lives on in its new form. It ends removed fields, running their `drop`, each as a call (`[RC-8]`):
  * at a host's poll, where no thread runs Ember code, at once;
  * at `std.hot.checkpoint()`, when that call is accepted there, judged with `[HR-44]`'s facts of the frames below the checkpoint: the locks they hold, what they walk and view, and their contracts;
  * otherwise at the first later poll or checkpoint where the call is accepted.

  Under `ember run --hot`, whose only polls are checkpoints (`[HR-33]`), the reload report names each drop that waits and what keeps it out: \"12 removed `Log` values wait: `Log`'s `drop` takes `world.lock`, which `main` holds at the checkpoint on line 21; call `std.hot.checkpoint()` after the `with world.lock:` block\". Prepare runs no check point: a `migrate_from` is compiled with none, since prepare ends nothing (`[HR-2]`)."

* `[HR-3b]` *(changed)* Adds: "`std.hot.checkpoint()` is a check point (`[RC-4]` point 3), and it empties its thread's queue first when it is clear. A layout change of a type whose values may be queued to this thread applies only when that queue is empty. Every other thread is outside Ember code, so it is at rest and has nothing queued. Otherwise the change is not applied at this checkpoint: the report names the line that kept the queue from being emptied, and the change applies at the next checkpoint or poll where the queue is empty."

* `[RT-8]` *(changed)* Adds:
  * "Entering rest is one compare-and-exchange of the thread's queue word, from empty to at rest. It is a release. When values arrived, the thread empties them and tries again.
  * A taker registers with one atomic add to the thread's taker count, then reads the queue word again. When it finds the thread leaving rest, it deregisters and pushes as usual.
  * Leaving rest is one atomic or of the leaving mark into the queue word, then a wait until the taker count is zero.
  * Registering and the read after it, and the leaving mark and the wait after it, are sequentially consistent, so each side sees the other. Deregistering is a release, and the wait reads the count with acquire, so the thread leaving rest sees every count and mark a taker wrote.
  * The protocol is stress-tested as rule Q was (`stress.c`)."

* `[COST-3]` *(changed)*
  * The owner-count row: "... for `thread_shared` on the thread that made the value until it is handed over (`[RC-4]`). A value whose drops may wait or call C is handed over where it is made (`[RC-8]` point 2) ..."
  * The two-count row:
    * "A test of the thread's queue at each check point: at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts, and once every N rounds of a loop whose count is known, so that the rounds between two tests stay vectorisable.
    * There is no test inside a function under a contract the queued drops would break, or inside a walk or a view they clash with (`[RC-8]`).
    * One compare-and-exchange to enter rest, and one atomic or with a load to leave it. These are paid only when a job worker sleeps for lack of work, on a blocking call's sleeping path, around a foreign call that may block, and around an outermost call from C whose code may touch a home count; and only on a thread whose code may make a value that can be queued.

Main never runs `~Conn()`. A drop that main does run for another thread (one that neither waits nor calls C) waits for nothing, so main's walk under `pool.lock` is never interrupted by a wait for that lock, nor by a change to the walked list. Nothing is refused and nothing is written.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # takes a lock, so it may wait
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])   # counted like a shared_ptr from here
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the worker ends the Conn's last owner and runs ~Conn() there
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:
            for id in pool.free:              # no drop main runs for another thread waits here
                println(id)
    println(h.join())
answers.outcome: Compiles. While the worker runs, frames print nothing, because `pool.free` is empty. When the worker's function ends, `b` ends and with it the `Conn`'s last owner, so the worker runs `~Conn()`. It waits for `pool.lock` until main's current `with` block ends, then pushes 1. Every later frame prints 1, and `h.join()` prints 1. `~Conn()` never runs on main, so main never waits for its own lock, and the list it walks never changes under it. Every count change of a `Conn` is one atomic add or subtract, as a `shared_ptr`'s is.

method1_repair.prior_art:
**C++ and Rust.** A `shared_ptr`'s destructor, and an `Arc`'s drop, run where the last owner ends, on that thread, with an atomic count on every thread. Point 2 gives exactly that to a drop that waits or calls C: it runs at the place a programmer can see. In both languages, a self-wait there is found only at run time. A destructor that locks a `std::mutex` its own thread holds is undefined behaviour, and Rust's `Mutex` docs say that locking it twice "might panic or deadlock". Ember refuses that self-wait when compiling (`[THR-19]`).

**Python.** CPython runs `__del__` wherever a count reaches zero or the collector runs. Its data-model documentation warns that `__del__` may run in the middle of arbitrary code, on any thread, so one that takes a lock or waits can deadlock on the code it interrupted. Point 2 removes exactly that hazard.

**Swift.** SE-0371's isolated deinit queues the deinit of an actor-isolated object released elsewhere as a job on the actor's executor, so it runs between jobs. That is the shape of point 3, but only for actor classes, and with no compile-time check.

**Go, Java, .NET.** Finalisers and cleaners run on a runtime thread. Go runs all of them in one goroutine, in order, and its docs tell a long finaliser to start its own goroutine. There is no time bound, and a collector is needed. This is option D.

**crossbeam-epoch.** It runs deferred destructors during a later `pin()` on any thread, with no time bound.

**Biased counting** (Choi, Shull and Torrellas, PACT 2018), where Ember's two counts come from, leaves it to the runtime when the owner thread processes its queue. The BRC report says the placement is "still to design".

**Threads in native code.** The JVM treats a thread running native code as being at a safepoint: the VM goes on without it, and the thread checks on its way back. Go's scheduler hands a goroutine's processor on while it sits in a blocking system call or a cgo call. Point 6's rest is the same idea, applied to the queue.

**Loop polls.** HotSpot polls at loop back edges. In counted loops it polls once every so many rounds (loop strip mining), so the rounds in between stay optimisable. Point 3 places tests the same way.

**Linux.** The last `fput()` of a file defers the release to task_work, which runs when the task returns to user mode, where it holds no kernel lock. RCU callbacks must not sleep. These are the two halves of the rule: a deferred end runs where it clashes with nothing, and only an end that does not wait is deferred.

**Objective-C/Cocoa.** An autorelease pool is drained at the top of each run-loop turn.

**C#.** `await` inside a `lock` statement is refused (CS1996). This bears on the lock-across-`yield` question raised for `[THR-19]`.

**Where each falls short.**
* C++ and Rust pay an atomic count for every type and leave self-waits to run time.
* The finaliser-thread languages give no bound and need a collector.
* Swift, Cocoa and Linux get the right shape, but by convention or for one kind of object.

The rule decides, when compiling, which ends may be deferred at all (those that neither wait nor call C). It places them where they clash with nothing, and keeps the two-count speed for them.
method1_repair.cost:
**Against what.** C has no deferred ends and pays nothing here. The relevant comparison is one atomic count (C++ `shared_ptr`, Rust `Arc`). Verdict 101's two counts beat it by 25% on a thread's own objects: 32.6 ms against 43.6 ms (`measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md`, own pattern, one thread). The rule keeps that gain for every type whose drop neither waits nor calls C. A type whose drop does either pays exactly C++'s and Rust's cost.

**Per operation.**
1. **A check point outside a clash:** one thread-local load of the queue word, and a branch not taken. It sits at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts. A loop whose trip count is known gets one every N rounds, so the rounds in between stay one loop the C compiler can vectorise. This is fewer tests than today's test at every back edge.
2. **Inside a function under a contract the queued drops would break, or a walk or view they clash with:** zero, because no point is placed there. A lock no longer keeps points out: queued drops take none.
3. **Where such a region ends, if it kept a point out:** one thread-local load and a branch.
4. **A direct call from such a region into a function that has points:** zero time. The cost is one more copy of the function, in code size, as with verdict 88's copy, and only for callees that have points.
5. **Calls from such a region that may reach points:** one plain thread-local add before the call and one subtract after. This covers a call through a function value or a `dyn`/`virtual` method, a foreign call that may run kept callbacks, and a call that may sleep or run jobs on this thread. The points read the mark only when the queue holds values.
6. **Rest:** one compare-and-exchange to enter it, and one atomic or with a load to leave it. It is paid only:
   * when a job worker sleeps for lack of work;
   * on a blocking call's sleeping path, beside the system call that sleeps;
   * around a foreign call that may block, beside the call;
   * around an outermost call from C whose code may touch a home count.

   And it is paid only on a thread whose code may make a value that can be queued. A foreign function that declares no effects counts as one that may block (`[EFF-3]`). Declaring its effects without `Block` removes the cost.
7. **Taking over a resting thread's value:** one atomic add and one subtract to register and deregister, plus the merge (one atomic add) that the maker would have done. Then comes the drop the value needs anyway. This is paid only on the path that would otherwise queue.
8. **A value whose drop may wait or call C:** one atomic add or subtract for every owner made or ended, on every thread, as `shared_ptr` does: 43.6 ms instead of 32.6 ms on the measurement's own-objects loop, for those types only. They have no queue, no placed point and no rest.
9. **A job worker before each job:** one thread-local load and a branch.

**Memory.** Zero per object: the 32-byte header already holds the queue link, and a type of item 8 keeps the same header. Per thread: the rest state in spare bits of the existing queue word, one taker count and one mark.

**Where it is zero.** Every count change of a type that may be queued; every check point outside a clash; every direct call; every exported function whose code touches no `thread_shared` count; every blocking call that does not sleep; every foreign call that neither may block nor runs callbacks inside a clash.

**Not measured:** items 6, 7 and 8 on real programs, and the choice of N. They must be measured on the laptop (P-cores, mains) before the rule goes in, and the rest protocol must be stress-tested the way `stress.c` tested rule Q.

readability.note: Not a character changes: the rule adds no word, attribute or line. The same text now has one meaning, and it is the meaning a C++ or Rust programmer expects. A destructor that takes a lock, waits, or calls C runs where its last owner ends. Any other destructor runs on its making thread, at a point that clashes with nothing, or at once while that thread is idle. The work belongs to the compiler (which types may be queued, and where the points go) and to the runtime (rest). The programmer never writes or sees any of it. A connection pool, a texture cache, a game loop and a C event loop read exactly as before. Option A would make the loop copy the list out of the lock.

method1_repair.compiler_does:
1. **Which types are handed over where they are made.** For each `thread_shared` type, the compiler works out its drop chain's effects: its drop and the drops of what it owns (`[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-24]`), with every implementation that may sit in an `owns dyn` field. A type whose chain may wait (`Block`) or call C (`FFI`) is handed over at every line that makes a value of it: the header starts with the owner in the away count and the handed-over mark, and every count change is atomic.
2. **Which types may be queued.** For every other `thread_shared` type, the compiler works out whether its values may be queued: whether an owner may reach another thread inside another object (by `[THR-2]`'s routes) without point 4's hand-over. For each thread entry (main, each `thread.spawn` and job function, each export and kept callback), it works out which such types the entry's code may make. Then it takes the summary of those queued drops: what they change and end, and their effects. One program-wide set is allowed.
3. **Which points are clear.** For each candidate point, it decides from each function's own code whether the point is clear: the function has no contract the drops' effects would break, and no live walk or view that they change or end. There is no lock condition.
4. **Context in callees.** It carries the caller's context into callees. A direct call made inside a region where the drops cannot run goes to a copy with no points. An indirect call, a foreign call that may run kept callbacks, or a call that may sleep or run jobs on this thread, made there, is bracketed by the thread-local mark.
5. **Where points go.** It places points at the back edges of loops whose trip count is not known when they start, and once every N rounds of counted loops (strip-mined). It also places them before blocking calls (blocking foreign calls included), where a region that kept a point out ends, at thread end, at the return to C, at a worker's wait, and before each job.
6. **Rest transitions.** It emits them at these places, and only on threads whose code may make a value that can be queued:
   * the return to C from an outermost call, with leaving rest on entry when the export's or callback's code may touch a home count;
   * around a foreign call that may block, with callbacks inside it leaving and re-entering rest when their code may touch a home count;
   * on a blocking call's sleeping path;
   * at a worker's wait;
   * at thread end.
7. **No effect from placed ends.** It keeps placed ends out of every effect set and summary, and refuses nothing because of them.
8. **Written ends.** It checks written ends as calls (point 1), every end of a handed-over type's last owner on any thread included (`[THR-20]`).
9. **Hot reload.** It records whether each `std.hot.checkpoint()` call is clear. It records `[HR-44]`'s facts for the frames below each checkpoint (the locks they hold, what they walk and view, their contracts), so that plan can time the drops of removed fields. It compiles each `migrate_from` with no points.
10. **Inspection (optional).** `ember inspect` lists each type handed over where it is made, with the operation in its drop that waits or calls C, and each point left out, with what kept it out.
method1_repair.misuse:
**Nothing new can be misused.** No program can write, call or skip a check point, choose which types are queued, or read the header (`[OBJ-1]`).

**Refused when compiling:** a written end that clashes.
* A local or a temporary ends inside `with pool.lock:`, and its drop takes `pool.lock`: `E7018`, with the line to write.
* The last owner of a `Conn` ends inside `with pool.lock:` on any thread. That line runs `~Conn()` (point 2), so it is `E7018` there.
* A `clear()` inside a walk of something its drops change: `E3020`.

**Never undefined behaviour, and no hidden wait.**
* A drop the compiler places never waits for anything and never calls C, because a drop that may do either is never placed. So neither C++'s self-wait on a `std::mutex` (undefined) nor a C call inside C's own locked dispatch can happen at a line the program did not write.
* A placed drop never runs inside a walk, a view or a contract it clashes with.
* Another thread reads a home count only while that count's thread rests, after a release. A taker runs no user code while it is registered.

**Not refused, and stated:**
* A thread that runs for ever where no point is clear (an endless loop inside `@noalloc` whose queued drops allocate) keeps its queued values until it leaves. Only memory is held, since those drops neither wait nor call C.
* A drop that waits runs where its last owner ends, and waits there, as in C++ and Rust. A self-wait on a std lock there is refused (`[THR-19]`). A cycle between threads built from the program's own waits is the program's, as in C++ and Rust; the debug lock-order report (`[THR-4]`) and `L7001` point at it.
* A wait built by hand from an `Atomic` (a spin loop) is not an operation the compiler sees as waiting. A queued drop that spins until its own making thread lets go hangs, as a spin lock taken twice does in C. std's locks and channels are seen.

A written end inside a lock, whose drop takes that lock, is refused when compiling (point 1), as 43 refuses any such call.

**56 kept.** A queued value is marked ended before its drop runs, on the making thread and on a taker alike, and links then find it gone.

**57 kept, and carried to every end.** Ending a value is a call of its drop where the drop runs. For an end the compiler places, the compiler puts it only where that call is accepted, so 57 holds for queued drops with nothing refused.

**101: the placement it left open, plus two changes that need the owner's yes.**
* **Kept:** the two numbers. The making thread deletes a queued value at its next check point, "placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends". The BRC report says the placement is "still to design", and decisions.md section 6 records the back-edge placement as a lead choice.
* **Widened:** "or the other thread deletes it at once if the making thread has ended" becomes "... is at rest". At rest means: ended, back in C, waiting for work, or asleep in a blocking call or a foreign call that may block. The evidence:
  * J7-02: a pool worker never ends, and a C thread may never call in again. Under 101's letter, a value queued to either is held for the life of the process.
  * A resting thread touches no home count, exactly like an ended one, so the same takeover is safe.
  * It costs nothing on any fast path.
* **Narrowed:** a type whose drop may wait or call C is handed over where it is made. This is 101's own fix 2 ("a hand-over the compiler sees moves A into B"), applied at the making line. All its counts are atomic, and it ends where its last owner ends. The evidence: three programs that work with `shared_ptr` and `Arc` fail under every placement on the making thread, because the making thread is the wrong thread to do the waiting:
  * a drop that sends on a bounded channel only its maker drains: the maker waits for itself;
  * a drop that takes a lock another thread holds while that thread waits for the maker: a cycle the text does not show;
  * a drop that calls C inside C's own locked dispatch: undefined behaviour, against a true `# SAFETY:` note.

  The cost: those types pay `shared_ptr`'s count, 43.6 ms against 32.6 ms on the measured own-objects loop. Every other type keeps 101's speed. This is narrower than option C, which counts every type whose drop reaches outside its fields, and everything a worker makes, atomically.

**114 kept.** An object moved to another thread has its drop run once there: a written end on that thread.

**164 to 166 untouched.** The rule relies on `[THR-8]` and `[THR-20]`: a `thread_shared` value's drop reaches only what any thread may reach.

**Not decided here:**
* Whether what a queued drop changes makes a `@deterministic` function `Nondet` is `[DET-2]`'s question, under P14's J6-07. The rule says only that timing alone is not `Nondet` (`[DET-6]`).
* A lock held across a `yield` is `[THR-19]`'s gap, raised separately.

method1_repair.open_risks:
1. **A lock held across a `yield` (outside P05, real).** A generator suspended inside a lock's `with` block holds that lock while its consumer runs. A written `with` of the same lock, or a written end whose drop takes it, in the consumer's loop is then a self-wait that `[THR-19]` does not see. This rule no longer depends on it, but the gap needs its own owner question. One option is to refuse a `yield` inside a lock's block or with a live guard, as CORO-13 does for `@must_drop` and as C# does for `await` in `lock`. The other is to count the lock as held while the frame may be suspended there.
2. **Speed of the types handed over where they are made.** It is unmeasured on real programs; the only number is the own-objects loop (43.6 against 32.6 ms). Every `thread_shared` wrapper of a C resource, and every type whose drop takes a lock or sends on a bounded channel, counts atomically. If std's console printing waits or calls C, every drop that prints is handed over too. That is correct, but it widens the set. Measure on the laptop (P-cores, mains).
3. **The rest protocol is a new concurrent protocol** on the queue word: compare-and-exchange to enter, takers that register, a leaving mark. It must be stress-tested the way `stress.c` tested rule Q (the race found there was in this very hand-over). Rest around foreign calls that may block and around callbacks must be measured. A foreign function that declares no effects counts as possibly blocking, so it pays rest on threads that may have queued values. No number here is measured.
4. **Code size.** Copies of functions called inside contract regions cost code size. Where size matters, the compiler may use the mark instead, at one thread-local add and one subtract per call.
5. **N for strip-mined counted loops** is unmeasured. A recursion with no loop reaches a point only when it returns to a loop or ends.
6. **Coordination with other groups.**
   * P14: `Block` must carry every operation that may wait. The table's row names receives and reads, not a bounded `send` or a static's first access. Whether what the queued drops change is `Nondet` is J6-07's question.
   * P09: the time of reclaim. Removed fields that are one-thread values of other threads must be ended before those threads enter Ember again (HR-42's publication).
   * P01: the rule relies on `[THR-8]` and `[THR-20]`.
7. **Output from a drop may come from main or from a worker**, depending on timing. That was already so.
8. **A thread that sleeps where its queue cannot be emptied** (a blocking call inside `@noalloc` whose queued drops allocate) rests with those values still queued. They wait for its first clear point after it wakes.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

static POOL_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut FREE: Array[int] guarded by POOL_LOCK = []
static mut BUSY: Array[int] guarded by POOL_LOCK = [7, 8]

gen fn busy_ids() -> Generator[int]:
    with POOL_LOCK:                 # still held while the generator waits at its yield
        for id in BUSY:
            yield copy of id

class Conn:
    id: int
    fn drop():
        with POOL_LOCK:
            FREE.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the worker ends the Conn's last owner: queued to main
    for frame in 0..1000:

No rule refuses `yield` inside a lock's `with` block: CORO-13 refuses only a live @must_drop value. A `with g = m.lock():` guard of a parameter held across a yield does the same (CORO-6). holes.what_goes_wrong: Each Texture names its maker through its chunk's header, and every taker reads that thread's queue word, taker count and mark. The design says 'an ended thread is at rest for good'. It does not say that the thread's record lives as long as any value it made, or what happens when the allocator hands its chunks, or the OS its id, to a new thread. Such a thread would merge and end values another entry made, at points placed for the types its own entry makes (compiler_does 2 allows per-entry sets). Separately, FFI-22's change has `ember_rt_shutdown()` 'end what is still queued to each thread' with no condition that those threads are at rest. It may then merge the home counts of a thread still running, a data race.
holes.fix_hint: A thread's record (queue word, taker count, mark) lives until no chunk names it and is never given to another thread. A chunk is never handed to a thread of another entry while per-entry sets are used, or one program-wide set is required. ember_rt_shutdown ends only the queues of threads at rest, and waits (or reports) while a thread runs Ember code.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock, channel

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    tx, rx = channel[thread_shared Conn](capacity=64)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: for c in rx: println(c.id))
    for i in 0..1000000:
        c = thread_shared Conn(id=i, pool=thread_shared pool)
        if i % 1000 == 0:
            tx.send(owns c).expect("receiver is gone")   # a hand-over of RC-4 point 4
    mem.drop(owns tx)
    h.join()
holes.what_goes_wrong: No `Conn` can ever be queued: the only route to another thread is the channel, a hand-over the compiler sees (verdict 101 fix 2, RC-4 point 4), and no `Conn` travels inside another object. Yet RC-8 point 2 (and compiler_does step 1) hands every `Conn` over at its making line only because `~Conn()` takes a lock, so the 999,000 Conns that live and end on main pay an atomic count instead of the plain home count. That is the design's own 43.6 ms against 32.6 ms on the own-objects loop, for a type whose waiting drop is never at risk. Step 2 already works out which types may be queued and does not use it here. P03's principle also chooses storage at the making line from what the program later does with the value.
holes.fix_hint: Hand a type over where it is made only when its drop chain may wait or call C AND its values may be queued (step 2's analysis: an owner may reach another thread inside another object without a point-4 hand-over). Every other lock-taking or C-calling type keeps 101's two counts. State it in RC-8 point 2, the COST-3 owner-count row and `ember inspect`'s list.

holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-4 point 3 and compiler_does step 5 place a test of the thread's queue at every back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known, and every N rounds of a counted loop, in every function of every program. The two-count COST-3 row keeps it 'guaranteed present'. The compiler already works out, per thread entry, which queueable types the entry's code may make (step 2), and uses that only to skip rest transitions (step 6). So a program with no queueable type, or a function reachable only from such threads, still pays a load of a word other threads write and a branch on every round of every `while`. C pays nothing. The C compiler may not hoist that load, so it also stops vectorising early-exit search loops like this one. The cost section contradicts itself: item 1 prices a check point outside a clash at one load and a branch, while 'Where it is zero' lists 'every check point outside a clash'.
holes.fix_hint: Place no check point (and no strip mining) in code that runs only on threads to which no value can be queued; with no queueable type in the program, place none at all. Make the COST-3 row 'guaranteed elided' there, and correct 'Where it is zero'.

unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn hypot(x: c_double, y: c_double) -> c_double      # no @ffi(effects=[...])

fn lengths(xs: Span[f64], ys: Span[f64], ref mut out: MutSpan[f64]):
