# main also makes thread_shared Texture values that reach a worker inside a Bundle (J7-02's shape)
holes.what_goes_wrong: A foreign function that states no effects has every effect (FFI-10, EFF-3), so under RC-4 point 6 and FFI-22 it 'may block'. On a thread whose code may make a queueable value, every one of the n calls is wrapped in a compare-and-exchange to enter rest and an atomic or with a load to leave it, all sequentially consistent (RT-8). C, Rust and COST-3's own 'FFI call' row ('one direct call for an ABI-direct C function', which the design leaves unchanged) pay one call. The cost buys nothing for safety, only a shorter wait for values queued during the call. It falls on the ordinary game or numeric loop, and the only way out is a word the programmer must add, `@ffi(effects=[], no_callbacks)`. The same two atomics are paid at the entry and return of every outermost call from C whose code may touch a home count, such as a per-entity `on_update` export.
holes.fix_hint: Rest around a foreign call only when its effects include Block as declared; an undeclared call leaves the thread running, and values queued meanwhile end at its first point after the return. Or give rest a fast path of plain thread-local stores, with the rare taker paying a process-wide barrier (FlushProcessWriteBuffers or membarrier, as HotSpot's and .NET's native-state transitions do), reusing HR-42's Ember-depth counter, which already marks a thread outside Ember code. Either way, update COST-3's FFI and export rows.

holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-8 point 3 calls a point clear when 'a call of its drops, written there, would be accepted'. `~Texture()` has no Sync, so the strip-mined points inside `scale` are clear. When the worker's end queues the Texture, main empties its queue inside `scale`: an acquire exchange of the queue word, and an atomic add merging the home count into the away count (ending a thread_shared owner). Both are the Sync that `@nosync` forbids (EFF table; EFF-1 counts an operation's count changes as its effects). An end written there would be E4002. `@nosync` is in EFF-14's usual inner-loop set, so the contract is broken at lines the program never wrote, against P14's principle that a contract means all of what it says.
holes.fix_hint: Test a point as 'the end of such a value, written there': the drops plus the end's own work (the queue's exchange and the merge, Sync). Then no point is placed inside @nosync code, and those inner loops carry no test at all.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Main empties its queue at a point and runs a Mesh's drop. Its loop over 1000 names reaches a strip-mined check point, which is clear and finds more Meshes the worker has just ended, so it empties the queue again inside that drop. That drop's loop does the same. Nothing in RC-4 points 2, 3 or 6 stops a point inside a drop the emptying runs from emptying again. While the worker ends Meshes faster than main finishes N names, the nesting deepens. Main never returns to its own loop, and the stack grows until 'stack overflow' aborts the program (RT-12). A flat emptying, or C++ freeing each Mesh on the worker, finishes.
holes.fix_hint: The emptying sets the thread's mark (RC-4 point 3) for its length. A point inside a drop it runs then leaves newly queued values for the emptying loop, which takes them after each drop, or for the next point once this snapshot is done. That gives constant stack, main keeps making progress, and the fast path costs nothing.

holes.what_goes_wrong: `~GpuBuffer()` has neither Block nor FFI, so it is queued to main. It then runs at a back edge of main's frame loop and spins until main sets `done`, which main does only after the loop: the program hangs. In C++ or Rust the worker spins until main sets the flag, and the program finishes. A drop that takes a lock without waiting has the same problem: `try_lock` has the Lock effect (EFF-21), but point 2 looks only at Block. Run at main's point inside main's own `with pool.lock:`, it always fails, so the id is silently never given back. That contradicts the design's 'no queued drop takes a lock'. The design lists the spin as a limitation, but the compiler can see the cause: a loop in the drop chain whose exit test reads memory another thread writes (an Atomic load, try_lock, try_recv).
holes.fix_hint: Count as 'may wait' in RC-8 point 2 every drop chain that takes a lock in any form (the Lock effect, try_lock included), or that contains a loop whose exit depends on a value another thread may write (an Atomic load, try_lock, try_recv in the condition). Such types end where their last owner ends, as C++ runs them. The limitation then leaves `misuse`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2 decides what a making line does (all counts atomic from the start, and which thread runs the drop) from facts worked out from drop bodies, including every implementation that may sit in an `owns dyn` field. EFF-25 and BLD-14 say a fact worked out from a body 'never changes what a line does: it decides only whether a line compiles, or removes a test'. Here an edit inside `~Saver()` silently moves drops between threads and changes their cost. Across a package edge the decision cannot be made at all: `make_host`'s making line is generated with the library, which cannot see the program's `Saver`. So a `Host` that travels inside an object is queued to main with a drop that may wait. Since RC-8 point 3 has 'no lock condition', that drop can run at main's back edge inside `with journal.lock:`, which is J7-01's self-wait again.
holes.fix_hint: State point 2 as an exception to EFF-25, with its reason (principle 6). Record 'drop may wait or call C' per type in the interface file. Decide it where the making line is compiled: either an `owns dyn` field of an interface other packages may implement counts as may-wait unless every implementation is known there, or the making line reads one flag from the type's information, which the program's final link sets from every implementation.

from std.sync import Receiver

class Buffer:
    samples: Array[f32] = []

static RETURNED: Receiver[thread_shared Buffer] = audio_returns()   # buffers the mixer gives back

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `on_audio`
@unsafe(export("on_audio", threads=any))
@realtime
pub extern "C" fn on_audio(frames: i32) -> i32:
    if RETURNED.try_recv() exists as b:     # b, a thread_shared owner, ends at the block's end
        return frames
    return 0
holes.what_goes_wrong: `on_audio`'s code may end a thread_shared owner, so by RC-4 point 6 and FFI-22 it 'leaves rest on entry': an atomic or of the leaving mark, then 'a wait until the taker count is zero'. Another thread may have registered as a taker of this driver thread's queue an instant before, and been preempted inside its few instructions. Then the @realtime (@noblock) callback waits on another thread's progress at a line the compiler placed. Placed work is in no effect set, so no contract sees it. This is the one wait the count protocol adds; rule Q's push and the merge are lock-free.
holes.fix_hint: Make leaving rest wait-free. A taker publishes the value it is merging in a per-taker slot, and the thread leaving rest completes that merge itself with the same CAS steps (helping), instead of waiting. Or takers claim each value with a CAS on its away word, so the maker never waits for another thread.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Points are placed so that a running thread never runs an unbounded number of loop rounds without one. Unbounded work without loops is not covered: 'a recursion with no loop reaches a point when it returns to one'. For the whole of `fib(50)`, or a recursive tree walk or recursive-descent parse of a large input, main reaches no point and does not rest. Every value queued to it meanwhile is held until the computation ends. The rule's own claim, a bound on when a queued value ends, does not hold for this ordinary shape.
holes.fix_hint: Also place a point at the entry (or return) of every function in a recursive group, tested like a back edge, as HotSpot polls at method returns. Strip it like a counted loop (every N calls, with a thread-local counter) if the test shows on calls.

import std.thread

class Texture:
    id: int

class Bundle:
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn main():
    t = thread_shared Texture(id=1)
    b = Bundle(textures=[thread_shared t])           # main's home count: 2
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.textures.len())
    println(h.join())   # main sleeps in join, so it rests; the worker's end of b takes over: 2 + (-1) = 1
    println(t.id)       # t ends at main's end
holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-4 point 6 says the taker 'adds the value's home count into its away count, marks the value ended when the sum is zero, and deregisters'. It says nothing for a non-zero sum, like this one. Main still owns `t`, and its later `-1` is a plain subtract of the home count (RT-10), which the taker has already folded into the away count. Read as written, either main's owner is counted twice and the Texture never ends (a leak), or an implementation that zeroes only one side ends it while `t` still points at it. Today's point 2 has the same gap for the maker's own merge, and the design copies it into the new take-over path.
holes.fix_hint: State that after any merge, by the maker or by a taker, the home count is zero and the value is marked handed over, so every later owner end (the maker's included) is an atomic subtract of the away count, and the subtract that reaches zero ends it at its line.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2's list of what 'may wait' (a lock, a bounded send, a receive, a join, a sleep, a static's first access) leaves out a blocking write or flush. The EFF table's Block row names only 'a blocking receive or read', so this drop is Io, not Block, and is queued to main. When the pipe is full, `~Report()` waits at main's back edge for a reader that is main: the bounded-send self-wait again, through a file. Where main is not the reader, the write still stalls main's loop, where C++ would stall the worker. The design tells P14 only about the bounded send and the static.
holes.fix_hint: Define 'may wait' by what the operation does, as P14's principle asks: a blocking write or flush (file, pipe, socket, console) included. List it in RC-8 point 2, and give it to P14 with the bounded send. If console output can wait, J7-02's Texture is then handed over too, and its answer text should say so.
